record.body: An autonomous recording unit, or ARU, is a weatherproof recorder with a microphone, battery, and memory that runs unattended on a programmed schedule for weeks or months, and arrays of ARUs spread across a landscape let researchers monitor many sites at once. Arrays can also localise callers: when the same call reaches several recorders at slightly different times, the time differences reveal the caller's position, a technique called acoustic localisation. ARUs transformed soundscape ecology because they remove the observer effect, record through the night and in bad weather, and produce comparable samples across sites. Their limits are real: batteries and memory run out, microphones degrade, and a recorder hears only its own small radius, so array design, spacing, and maintenance are part of the science. ARU recordings contain all three layers, and analysis separates biophony from geophony and anthrophony.
